blueprint.title: Chapter 1: Mobile Computing & Android Architecture (CoSc4083 / ITec4103)

structured_notes.title: Smart Devices & Mark Weiser's Ubiquitous Computing Taxonomy
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Smart Devices & Mark Weiser's Classification
A **smart device** is digital, active, computer-networked, user-reconfigurable, and capable of operating to some extent autonomously.

| Category | Physical Scale | Usage Form | Slide Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tabs** | Centimeter-sized ($\text{cm}$) | Accompanied or wearable devices | Smartphones, smart cards |
| **Pads** | Decimeter-sized ($\text{dm}$) | Hand-held devices | Laptops |
| **Boards** | Meter-sized ($\text{m}$) | Interactive display surfaces | Horizontal surface computers, vertical smart boards |

structured_notes.title: Core Characteristics of Mobile Devices
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Mobile Device Architectural Properties
- **Mobility**: Loosely-bound vs. tightly-bound to users.
- **Locus of Control**: Resides **inside the smart device**.
- **Connectivity**: Intermittent resource access over local/wide-area wireless networks.
- **Intelligence**: Personalized single portal with **context awareness**.

structured_notes.title: Feature Phone vs. Smartphone & Hardware Constraints
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Feature Phone vs. Smartphone
- **Feature Phone**: Runs on **proprietary firmware** and limited platforms.
- **Smartphone**: Runs an **open and complete mobile operating system**, tightly integrates with UI and phone features, and relies on a powerful **API**.
- **Smartphone Constraints (Cons)**: Limited battery life, CPU speed, RAM, screen size, permanent storage, unreliable/slow network access with high latency, and inconsistent platforms.

structured_notes.title: Mobile Web Apps vs. Native Apps & Native SDK Languages
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Mobile App Paradigms & Native Platforms

| Platform / Environment | Native Programming Language(s) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Android / BlackBerry / Java ME** | Java |
| **iPhone (iOS)** | Objective-C |
| **Symbian** | C++ |
| **Qualcomm BREW** | C or C++ |
| **Windows Mobile (.NET Compact Framework)** | C++, C#, VB.NET |

structured_notes.title: Android History, Open Handset Alliance & Linux Kernel
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Milestones
- **Oct 2003**: Android, Inc. founded in Palo Alto, California.
- **Aug 2005**: Google acquired Android Inc.
- **Nov 2007**: **Open Handset Alliance (OHA)** unveiled Android built on **Linux Kernel version 2.6**.
- **Oct 2008**: Android OS released as open source.

structured_notes.title: Android Version Evolution & Milestone Features
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Key Android Version Milestones
- **1.5 Cupcake / 1.6 Donut** (2009): Initial releases.
- **2.0/2.1 Eclair**: HTML5 support, Geolocation API.
- **2.2 Froyo**: Chrome V8 JavaScript engine, Wi-Fi tethering, Adobe Flash support.
- **2.3 Gingerbread**: Near Field Communication (NFC).
- **3.0–3.2 Honeycomb**: Tablet-oriented release, multicore processor support, hardware-accelerated graphics, USB host transfer.
- **4.0 Ice Cream Sandwich**: Unified Gingerbread (phone) and Honeycomb (tablet).
- **4.1 Jelly Bean / 4.4 KitKat (API Level 19)**.

structured_notes.title: Four Categories of Android Applications
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Application Behavioral Types
1. **Foreground Activity**: Useful only when visible in foreground; effectively suspended otherwise.
2. **Background Service**: Limited user interaction; spends most of its lifetime hidden (e.g., call screening, SMS auto-responder).
3. **Intermittent Activity**: Expects some interactivity but does most work in the background (e.g., **media player**).
4. **Widgets**: Interactive visual components placed on the user's home screen (e.g., battery level, weather, clock).

structured_notes.title: Behavior Police & Process Assassin (ANR Thresholds)
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Responsiveness Thresholds (Slide 40)
The Android OS monitors two strict conditions (Process Assassin / ANR):
1. **User Action Response**: An Activity must respond to any user action (e.g., key press or touch) within **5 seconds**.
2. **BroadcastReceiver Timeout**: A `BroadcastReceiver` must return from its `onReceive()` handler within **10 seconds**.

structured_notes.title: Android Emulator (AVD) Default Hardware Characteristics & Snapshots
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Default AVD Hardware Parameters (Slides 48–51)
- **Device RAM size**: `96` MB
- **Camera support**: `no` (default max resolution `640x480`)
- **Cache partition size**: `66MB`
- **Abstracted LCD density**: `160` dpi
- **Snapshot Enabled**: Saves emulator state to a snapshot file on close so the next launch restores state almost instantly.

structured_notes.title: HTML5 Mobile Viewport, CSS Browser Engines & Web Storage
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Browser Rendering Engines & CSS Vendor Prefixes (Slide 52)

| Browser | Rendering Engine | CSS Vendor Prefix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Internet Explorer (IE)** | Trident | `-msie` |
| **Firefox** | Gecko | `-moz` |
| **Opera** | Presto | `-o` |
| **Safari & Chrome** | WebKit | `-webkit` |

- **Viewport Meta Tag**: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, user-scalable=yes">`
- **HTML5 Local Storage**: `localStorage.setItem("foo", "test!");` and `localStorage.getItem("foo");`
- **HTML5 Geolocation**: `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(function_name)`

structured_notes.title: PhoneGap / Apache Cordova Hybrid Android Architecture
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### PhoneGap Android Setup & Lifecycle (Slides 54–58)
1. Copy `cordova.js` into `assets/www/`, `cordova.jar` into `libs/`, and `xml/` into `res/`.
2. In HTML (`assets/www/index.html`), listen for the `"deviceready"` event via `document.addEventListener("deviceready", onDeviceReady, true)` before calling native APIs like `navigator.notification.alert()`.
3. In Java, extend `DroidGap` instead of `Activity` and load the local asset via `super.loadUrl("file:///android_asset/www/index.html");`.

structured_notes.title: Android Project Directory Structure & R.java (aapt)
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Project Directories (Slide 60)
- `src/`: Java source packages and `.java` classes.
- `res/layout/`: XML screen layouts (`main.xml`).
- `res/values/`: `strings.xml` and localized string folders (`values-ar`, `values-fr`).
- `res/drawable-hdpi|mdpi|ldpi/`: Resolution-specific images.
- `assets/`: Raw non-media files (HTML, bundled databases) not assigned resource IDs.
- `gen/`: Contains auto-generated `R.java` created by **Android Asset Packaging Tool (`aapt`)**. Never edit `R.java` manually.

structured_notes.title: AndroidManifest.xml Versioning, SDK Bounds & MAIN Intent Action
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### AndroidManifest.xml Core Attributes (Slide 62)
- `android:versionCode`: Internal integer version number used by the system/Play Store to determine upgrades.
- `android:versionName` (`versionNumber`): `<major>.<minor>` string displayed to users.
- `minSdkVersion` / `targetSdkVersion` / `maxSdkVersion`: API compatibility bounds.
- `android.intent.action.MAIN`: Marks the entry-point Activity loaded first when the application launches.

structured_notes.title: Android Component Model, Process Isolation & Tasks
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### APK Isolation, Processes & Tasks (Slides 64–65)
- By default, **one Linux process is created per APK**, and APKs are isolated from one another.
- Inter-Process Communication (IPC) occurs via **Intents** or **AIDL**.
- A **Task** is a collection of related Activities capable of spanning multiple processes, maintaining its own UI back-history stack.
- **Command to inspect APK permissions**: `aapt dump permissions <package_name>.appname.apk`.

structured_notes.title: Core Android Application Components
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### The 5 Building Blocks (Slide 65)
1. **Activity**: Single visual screen for user interaction.
2. **Service**: Runs in the background without a visual UI (e.g., music playback, network fetching).
3. **Broadcast Receiver**: Listens for and responds to system/app broadcast announcements.
4. **Content Provider**: Manages shared access to structured app data (e.g., SQLite database) across applications.
5. **Intents**: Asynchronous messages requesting functionality from other activities or services.

structured_notes.title: Dalvik Virtual Machine (Register-Based) vs. Java Virtual Machine (Stack-Based)
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Dalvik VM vs. Standard JVM (Slides 72–73)

| Architectural Feature | Java Virtual Machine (JVM) | Dalvik Virtual Machine (DVM) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Execution Architecture** | **Stack-based** VM | **Register-based** VM (virtual registers) |
| **Executable Format** | `.class` bytecode files | `.dex` (Dalvik Executable) produced by `dx` tool |
| **Constant Pool** | Constants declared repeatedly per `.class` | Constants pooled and declared **only once** in `.dex` |
| **Performance & Size** | Larger uncompressed footprint | Up to **half the code size** and runs **~30% faster** |
| **GUI Libraries** | Supports Swing and AWT | Does **not** support Swing or AWT |
| **Standard C Library** | Standard GNU `glibc` | **Bionic** (custom stripped-down `libc` for Android) |

structured_notes.title: APK Packaging Format & Inspection Tools
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Inside an Android Package (`.apk`) (Slides 70–73)
- An `.apk` is a modified **Java Archive (`.jar`)** file.
- Contains compiled `.dex` bytecode, binary `AndroidManifest.xml`, compiled resources (`resources.arsc`), and uncompiled raw assets.
- **List `.apk` contents**: `jar tvf filename.apk`
- **Inspect `.dex` details**: `dexdump`

structured_notes.title: Deploying & Installing Apps via ADB on Physical Devices
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Device Deployment Requirements & ADB CLI (Slides 74–75)
1. Set `android:debuggable="true"` on the `<application>` tag in `AndroidManifest.xml`.
2. Enable **Unknown sources** (`Settings -> Applications`) and **USB Debugging** (`Settings -> Applications -> Development -> USB debugging`).
3. Manual CLI installation command:
   ```bash
   adb [-d | -e] install <path>/<file>.apk
   ```

structured_notes.title: Android Debugging Environment: DDMS, ADB & JDWP
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Core Debugging Tools (Slide 76)
- **DDMS (Dalvik Debug Monitoring Service)**: Graphical tool that captures screenshots, gathers thread and stack information, and spoofs incoming voice calls and SMS messages.
- **ADB (Android Debug Bridge)**: Command-line device management and APK installation bridge.
- **JDWP Debugger**: Java Debug Wire Protocol debugger used to step through code, inspect variable values, and set breakpoints.

structured_notes.title: Release Mode Packaging & Private Key Signing
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Publishing to Play Store (Slide 79)
- Debug builds are automatically signed by Eclipse/SDK using a temporary debug key.
- To distribute publicly on the Play Store, you must export an unsigned package (or build in **release mode**), sign the `.apk` with your **own private key**, and configure `versionCode`, `versionName`, `minSdkVersion`, and `targetSdkVersion`.

questions.question_text:
According to Mark Weiser's classification of ubiquitous computing smart devices, which table correctly maps **Tabs**, **Pads**, and **Boards** to their physical dimensions and device examples?

| Device Class | Physical Scale | Representative Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tabs** | Centimeter-sized | Smart phones, smart cards |
| **Pads** | Decimeter-sized | Hand-held laptops |
| **Boards** | Meter-sized | Horizontal surface computers, vertical smart boards |

options.label: A
options.text: Tabs are meter-sized interactive displays; Pads are centimeter-sized smart cards; Boards are decimeter-sized laptops.

options.label: B
options.text: Tabs are accompanied/wearable centimeter-sized devices; Pads are hand-held decimeter-sized devices; Boards are meter-sized interactive display devices.

options.label: C
options.text: Tabs are decimeter-sized laptops; Pads are centimeter-sized wearables; Boards are millimeter-sized neural implants.

options.label: D
options.text: Tabs, Pads, and Boards refer exclusively to cloud server rack dimensions rather than user-facing smart devices.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: Mark Weiser categorized ubiquitous computing smart devices into three physical scales: **Tabs** (accompanied/wearable centimeter-sized devices like smartphones and smart cards), **Pads** (hand-held decimeter-sized devices like laptops), and **Boards** (meter-sized interactive displays like surface computers and smart boards).
- **Why A and C are incorrect**: They swap the centimeter, decimeter, and meter scale definitions.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Weiser's taxonomy classifies ubiquitous user devices, not server racks.

questions.question_text: Which set of architectural characteristics accurately describes a smart mobile computing device?

options.label: A
options.text: Guaranteed continuous broadband access, zero local autonomy, and a locus of control that resides exclusively on a remote central server.

options.label: B
options.text: Personalized operation as a single portal, intermittent resource access, context awareness, and a locus of control that resides in the smart device.

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed non-reconfigurable firmware, absence of local application services, and strictly wired Ethernet connectivity.

options.label: D
options.text: Unlimited battery capacity, desktop-grade RAM, and immunity to network latency.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: Mobile smart devices are user-reconfigurable, autonomous, context-aware, operate with intermittent resource access, and maintain a **locus of control that resides inside the smart device**.
- **Why A and C are incorrect**: Mobile devices operate autonomously with local control rather than acting as dumb terminals dependent on continuous connectivity.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Mobile devices face strict battery, RAM, CPU, and network latency constraints.

questions.question_text: What is the primary architectural distinction between a **Feature Phone** and a **Smartphone**?

options.label: A
options.text: A feature phone runs on proprietary firmware with limited platform support, whereas a smartphone runs an open and complete mobile OS tightly integrated with the UI and a powerful third-party API.

options.label: B
options.text: A feature phone supports full native SDKs and multitasking, whereas a smartphone only executes SMS and voice calls.

options.label: C
options.text: A smartphone lacks GPS, accelerometers, and Wi-Fi hardware, whereas a feature phone requires all three.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no software difference; the distinction is based solely on battery voltage.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Feature phones use proprietary firmware with restricted extensibility, while smartphones provide an open, complete mobile operating system tightly integrated with device hardware and a comprehensive API.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Smartphones—not feature phones—combine PDA, GPS, accelerometer, web browser, and rich third-party SDK capabilities.

questions.question_text:
Match the native mobile platforms listed in the table below with their primary native development languages:

| Mobile Platform | Native Development Language(s) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Android & BlackBerry** | ? |
| **2. Symbian** | ? |
| **3. iPhone (iOS)** | ? |
| **4. Windows Mobile (.NET Compact Framework)** | ? |

options.label: A
options.text: 1 = Objective-C, 2 = Java, 3 = VB.NET, 4 = Python

options.label: B
options.text: 1 = Java, 2 = C++, 3 = Objective-C, 4 = C++, C#, VB.NET

options.label: C
options.text: 1 = C#, 2 = HTML5, 3 = Java ME, 4 = Objective-C

options.label: D
options.text: 1 = PHP, 2 = Ruby, 3 = Java, 4 = C

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: In classical native mobile development environments, Android, BlackBerry, and Java ME use **Java**; Symbian uses **C++**; iPhone uses **Objective-C**; Qualcomm BREW uses **C/C++**; and Windows Mobile (.NET Compact Framework) uses **C++, C#, and VB.NET**.
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: They mismatch the native SDK languages for Android, Symbian, iOS, and Windows Mobile.

questions.question_text: In November 2007, the **Open Handset Alliance (OHA)** unveiled Android as an open-source mobile platform built upon which underlying operating system kernel?

options.label: A
options.text: Windows NT Kernel 5.1

options.label: B
options.text: Linux Kernel version 2.6

options.label: C
options.text: FreeBSD Mach Microkernel

options.label: D
options.text: Symbian Real-Time Executive (EKA2)

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: The Open Handset Alliance unveiled Android in November 2007 built on top of **Linux kernel version 2.6**.
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: Android is powered by the Linux kernel, not Windows NT, Mach (used in iOS/macOS), or Symbian EKA2.

questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly pairs the Android OS release codename with the major platform capability it introduced?

options.label: A
options.text: Froyo (2.2) -> Chrome V8 JavaScript engine & Wi-Fi tethering; Gingerbread (2.3) -> Near Field Communication (NFC); Honeycomb (3.0) -> Tablet-oriented UI & multicore support; Ice Cream Sandwich (4.0) -> Unified Gingerbread and Honeycomb.

options.label: B
options.text: Cupcake (1.5) -> Tablet-only release; Honeycomb (3.0) -> First phone release; KitKat (4.4) -> Removed SQLite support.

options.label: C
options.text: Donut (1.6) -> Replaced Dalvik with JVM; Eclair (2.0) -> Dropped HTML5 and Geolocation APIs.

options.label: D
options.text: Gingerbread (2.3) -> Tablet-only release; Froyo (2.2) -> Merged Honeycomb and Jelly Bean.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Android 2.2 (Froyo) introduced the Chrome V8 JS engine and Wi-Fi tethering; Android 2.3 (Gingerbread) added NFC; Android 3.0 (Honeycomb) targeted tablets with multicore and hardware acceleration support; and Android 4.0 (Ice Cream Sandwich) combined Gingerbread and Honeycomb.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: They misattribute version numbers and features across the Android release timeline.

questions.question_text: A developer builds an Android **Music Player** application where the user selects a playlist on screen, locks the phone, and continues listening while the app runs silently in the background and posts track notifications. Under which Android application category does this app fall?

options.label: A
options.text: Foreground-Only Activity

options.label: B
options.text: Intermittent Activity

options.label: C
options.text: Pure Home Screen Widget

options.label: D
options.text: Static Content Provider

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: An **Intermittent Activity** expects some user interactivity (selecting songs/playlists) but performs most of its work in the background (audio playback), notifying the user when appropriate.
- **Why A is incorrect**: A Foreground Activity is suspended whenever it is not visible.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: A media player is not merely a passive home-screen widget or database provider.

questions.question_text: Android's OS process manager ("Behavior police – Process assassin") monitors application responsiveness and terminates unresponsive components. What are the two exact timeout thresholds enforced by the OS?

options.label: A
options.text: Must respond to any user action (e.g., key press) within 5 seconds, and a BroadcastReceiver must return from its onReceive() handler within 10 seconds.

options.label: B
options.text: Must respond to any user action within 60 seconds, and a BroadcastReceiver must return within 120 seconds.

options.label: C
options.text: Must respond to any user action within 10 milliseconds, and a Service must stop within 1 second.

options.label: D
options.text: Must respond to a BroadcastReceiver within 5 seconds, and a user key press within 30 seconds.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Android enforces two strict responsiveness rules: (1) an application must respond to any user action such as a key press or touch within **5 seconds**, and (2) a `BroadcastReceiver` must finish and return from its `OnReceive` handler within **10 seconds**.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: They state incorrect timeout durations or swap the Activity and BroadcastReceiver thresholds.

questions.question_text: When configuring an Android Virtual Device (AVD) in the Android Emulator, what is the purpose of enabling the **Snapshot Enabled** option, and what are the default values for **Device RAM size**, **Cache partition size**, and **Abstracted LCD density**?

options.label: A
options.text: Snapshot saves emulator state on close so the next launch restores almost instantly; defaults are RAM = 96 MB, Cache = 66 MB, Abstracted LCD density = 160.

options.label: B
options.text: Snapshot takes JPEG photos using the webcam; defaults are RAM = 4096 MB, Cache = 512 MB, Abstracted LCD density = 480.

options.label: C
options.text: Snapshot compiles Java to C++; defaults are RAM = 16 MB, Cache = 0 MB, Abstracted LCD density = 72.

options.label: D
options.text: Snapshot deletes the SD card after every boot; defaults are RAM = 1024 MB, Cache = 128 MB, Abstracted LCD density = 320.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Checking **Snapshot Enabled** saves the AVD's runtime state to a snapshot file when closed so subsequent launches appear almost instantly instead of performing a full cold boot. The default hardware parameters are Device RAM size = `96` MB, Cache partition size = `66MB`, and Abstracted LCD density = `160`.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Misstate both the purpose of AVD snapshots and the default hardware configuration values.

questions.question_text:
Examine the following HTML5 mobile web tags and JavaScript snippets:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, user-scalable=yes">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes" />
```

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("foo", "test!");
var data = localStorage.getItem("foo");
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(showPosition);
```

Which browser rendering engine and CSS vendor prefix table correctly matches mobile and desktop browsers?

options.label: A
options.text: Safari & Chrome -> Engine: WebKit (-webkit); Firefox -> Engine: Gecko (-moz); Opera -> Engine: Presto (-o); IE -> Engine: Trident (-msie).

options.label: B
options.text: Safari & Chrome -> Engine: Trident (-msie); Firefox -> Engine: WebKit (-webkit); Opera -> Engine: Gecko (-moz).

options.label: C
options.text: Safari & Chrome -> Engine: Presto (-o); Firefox -> Engine: Trident (-msie); IE -> Engine: Gecko (-moz).

options.label: D
options.text: All browsers use the Dalvik engine and the -android CSS prefix.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Safari and Chrome use the **WebKit** layout engine (`-webkit` prefix), Firefox uses **Gecko** (`-moz`), Opera (classic) uses **Presto** (`-o`), and Internet Explorer uses **Trident** (`-msie`).
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Confuse browser layout engines and their corresponding CSS vendor prefixes.

options.label: A
options.text: cordova.js and index.html go in assets/www/, cordova.jar goes in libs/, and "deviceready" ensures the native PhoneGap/Cordova bridge has initialized before calling navigator.notification.alert().

options.label: B
options.text: cordova.js goes in res/values/, cordova.jar goes in gen/, and "deviceready" compiles Java files in the browser.

options.label: C
options.text: index.html goes in src/, and MainActivity must extend BroadcastReceiver instead of DroidGap.

options.label: D
options.text: super.loadUrl() downloads index.html over HTTP from Google Play Store on every launch.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: In a PhoneGap Android project, `cordova.js` and `index.html` reside in `assets/www/` (referenced at runtime via `file:///android_asset/www/index.html`), `cordova.jar` is placed in `libs/`, `xml/` goes into `res/`, and `MainActivity` extends `DroidGap`. Waiting for "deviceready" ensures the native Java-to-JavaScript bridge is ready before invoking `navigator.notification.alert()`.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Misstate the directory locations and how `file:///android_asset/` loads bundled local files.

questions.question_text:
In an `AndroidManifest.xml` file, an `<activity>` element includes the following attribute:

```xml
<activity
    android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:configChanges="orientation|keyboardHidden|keyboard|screenSize|locale">
```

What is the effect of declaring these `android:configChanges` flags on the Activity?

options.label: A
options.text: It locks the phone screen physically so the user can never rotate the device or change the system language.

options.label: B
options.text: It informs Android that the Activity will handle orientation, keyboard, screen size, and locale changes itself rather than having the OS destroy and restart the Activity by default.

options.label: C
options.text: It grants the application root permission to reformat external storage.

options.label: D
options.text: It deletes R.java whenever the screen rotates.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: Declaring `android:configChanges="orientation|keyboardHidden|keyboard|screenSize|locale"` prevents the default Android behavior of destroying and recreating the Activity on those runtime configuration changes, allowing the Activity/WebView container (such as PhoneGap's `DroidGap`) to stay intact.
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: `configChanges` neither locks orientation (which is `android:screenOrientation`) nor grants storage permissions.

questions.question_text: In a standard Android project structure, how is the `gen/R.java` file created, and what happens if a developer accidentally deletes `R.java`?

options.label: A
options.text: It is written manually by the developer; if deleted, the project is permanently corrupted and must be rewritten from scratch.

options.label: B
options.text: It is auto-generated by the Android Asset Packaging Tool (aapt) from the project's XML resources and manifest; if deleted, aapt automatically regenerates it on the next build.

options.label: C
options.text: It is downloaded from the Android Market when the user installs the app.

options.label: D
options.text: It contains raw MP3 and HTML files that belong in the assets/ folder.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: `gen/R.java` is auto-generated by the **Android Asset Packaging Tool (`aapt`)** to index resource IDs (`@layout`, `@string`, `@drawable`). Developers must never modify `R.java` manually, and if deleted, the build system automatically regenerates it.
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: `R.java` is a build-time generated Java class, not a manually written file or raw asset folder.

questions.question_text: How does Android support multi-language localization for UI text, and what is the role of `android.intent.action.MAIN` inside `AndroidManifest.xml`?

options.label: A
options.text: Strings are referenced via @string from res/values/strings.xml with translated folders like res/values-ar and res/values-fr; android.intent.action.MAIN designates the first Activity loaded when the application runs.

options.label: B
options.text: A separate APK must be compiled in C++ for every language; android.intent.action.MAIN uninstalls previous versions.

options.label: C
options.text: Translations are hardcoded inside R.java; android.intent.action.MAIN starts a background ContentProvider.

options.label: D
options.text: Strings are stored in bin/classes.dex only; android.intent.action.MAIN enables USB debugging.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: UI layouts reference `@string` variables defined in `res/values/strings.xml`, allowing locale-specific resource directories such as `res/values-ar` (Arabic) and `res/values-fr` (French) to supply translated strings automatically. In `AndroidManifest.xml`, `android.intent.action.MAIN` marks the entry Activity launched first when the app starts.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Android externalizes strings in XML resources rather than hardcoding them in `R.java` or requiring separate C++ builds.

questions.question_text: Which command-line tool and syntax inspects and dumps the permission details declared inside a compiled `.apk` package, and how does Android isolate APKs at runtime?

options.label: A
options.text: Command: aapt dump permissions <package_name>.appname.apk; by default, one Linux process is created per APK, APKs are isolated, and cross-process communication uses Intents or AIDL.

options.label: B
options.text: Command: javac -permissions app.apk; all installed APKs run inside a single shared Linux process with shared global variables.

options.label: C
options.text: Command: dexdump --grant-all app.apk; APKs communicate only by reading each other's private SQLite files directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Command: eclipse --dump-manifest; Android does not isolate processes.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: The Android Asset Packaging Tool command `aapt dump permissions <package_name>.appname.apk` prints the permissions requested by an APK. Under the Android Component Model, components within an APK share a single Linux process by default, APKs are isolated from each other, and inter-process communication (IPC) occurs via **Intents** or **AIDL**.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: APKs do not share a single global process or directly read private files across sandboxes.

questions.question_text: Which Android component provides a managed interface (often backed by a SQLite database) that supports sharing and accessing structured data across different applications?

options.label: A
options.text: Activity

options.label: B
options.text: Broadcast Receiver

options.label: C
options.text: Content Provider

options.label: D
options.text: Live Wallpaper

questions.explanation:
- **Why C is correct**: A **Content Provider** manages access to a structured set of data (such as a SQLite database) and provides the standard mechanism for sharing data securely across application boundaries.
- **Why A is incorrect**: An `Activity` represents a single visual screen for user interaction.
- **Why B is incorrect**: A `Broadcast Receiver` listens for and responds to broadcast announcements.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Live Wallpapers render animated home-screen backgrounds.

questions.question_text:
Compare the **Dalvik Virtual Machine (DVM)** used in Android with the standard **Java Virtual Machine (JVM)** across the architectural dimensions in the table below:

| Dimension | Standard JVM | Android Dalvik VM |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Instruction Architecture** | Stack-based | Register-based |
| **Bytecode File Format** | `.class` | `.dex` (generated by `dx`) |
| **Constant Pool Optimization** | Declared repeatedly per `.class` | Declared only once across `.dex` |
| **Standard C Library** | GNU `glibc` | `Bionic` |

Why does Dalvik's register-based `.dex` architecture outperform standard stack-based `.class` files on memory-constrained mobile devices?

options.label: A
options.text: Dalvik instructions operate directly on virtual registers (avoiding repetitive stack push/pop overhead) and deduplicate constants into a single pool, yielding compressed code up to half the size that runs roughly 30% faster.

options.label: B
options.text: Dalvik includes full desktop Swing and AWT libraries inside every .dex file to accelerate 3D gaming.

options.label: C
options.text: Dalvik is a stack-based VM that executes uncompiled .java text files directly without bytecode conversion.

options.label: D
options.text: Dalvik duplicates string constants in every method so garbage collection is never required.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Unlike the stack-based JVM, Dalvik is a **register-based VM** whose 16-bit instruction set works directly on variables in virtual registers, saving the time required to load/store variables to and from an operand stack. In addition, the `dx` utility pools constants so they are declared only once in the `.dex` file, resulting in code that is up to half the size and runs ~30% faster.
- **Why B is incorrect**: Swing and AWT are explicitly **not** supported by Dalvik.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: Dalvik is register-based (not stack-based) and declares constants only once.

questions.question_text: An `.apk` (Android Package) is a modified Java Archive (`.jar`) file generated into the project's `bin/` folder. Which files are packaged inside the `.apk`, and which CLI command lists the table of contents of `filename.apk`?

options.label: A
options.text: Contains compiled .dex files, binary AndroidManifest.xml, compiled resources (resources.arsc), and uncompiled resource files; inspected via: jar tvf filename.apk

options.label: B
options.text: Contains only raw .java source files and Eclipse .project files; inspected via: javac -list filename.apk

options.label: C
options.text: Contains Windows .dll libraries only; inspected via: ipconfig /all filename.apk

options.label: D
options.text: Contains uncompiled AndroidManifest.txt only; inspected via: ping filename.apk

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: An `.apk` archive packages the compiled Dalvik executable (`.dex`), a binary version of `AndroidManifest.xml`, compiled resources (`resources.arsc`), and uncompiled raw resource/asset files. Because an `.apk` is a modified `.jar` archive, running `jar tvf filename.apk` lists its contents (and `dexdump` inspects the `.dex` file).
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: `.java` source files are compiled into `.dex` before packaging, and `javac`/`ipconfig`/`ping` do not list archive contents.

questions.question_text: A developer wants to manually install a compiled `<file>.apk` onto a USB-connected physical Android phone or a running emulator from the command prompt using Android Debug Bridge (`adb`). Which prerequisites and command syntax are required?

options.label: A
options.text: Set android:debuggable="true" on <application>, enable "Unknown sources" and "USB debugging" on the device, and run: adb [-d | -e] install <path>/<file>.apk

options.label: B
options.text: Disable USB debugging, delete AndroidManifest.xml, and run: adb format-device <file>.apk

options.label: C
options.text: Copy the .java file to the SIM card and run: aapt run-usb <file>.java

options.label: D
options.text: Export an unsigned APK and open it inside Internet Explorer.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Running and debugging on a physical device requires setting `android:debuggable="true"` in `AndroidManifest.xml`, enabling **Unknown sources** (`Settings -> Applications`) and **USB debugging** (`Settings -> Applications -> Development`), and executing `adb [-d | -e] install <path>/<file>.apk` from `<sdk>/platform-tools/`.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Unsigned APKs cannot be installed, and `adb install` is the standard deployment command.

questions.question_text: In the Android debugging environment, what are the distinct responsibilities of **DDMS (Dalvik Debug Monitoring Service)**, **ADB (Android Debug Bridge)**, and the **JDWP Debugger**?

options.label: A
options.text: DDMS is a graphical tool that captures screenshots, gathers thread/stack info, and spoofs incoming calls/SMS; ADB provides device management and APK installation; JDWP steps through code, inspects variables, and pauses execution.

options.label: B
options.text: DDMS compiles XML layouts into R.java; ADB renders HTML5 pages in WebKit; JDWP signs release APKs for the Play Store.

options.label: C
options.text: DDMS is the relational database engine; ADB is the 3D graphics library; JDWP is the Linux kernel.

options.label: D
options.text: All three are aliases for the exact same CSS preprocessor.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: In the Android debugging toolchain: **DDMS** provides a GUI to capture screenshots, inspect threads/heap/stack, and spoof incoming calls or SMS messages; **ADB** manages device/emulator connections and package installation; and the **JDWP-compliant debugger** lets developers set breakpoints, pause execution, and inspect variable values.
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Confuse debugging tools with `aapt` (resource compiler), `SQLite` (database), and `OpenGL ES` (3D graphics).
